Title: Personalized oncogenomics: clinical experience with malignant peritoneal mesothelioma using whole genome sequencing
Abstract Summary: Peritoneal mesothelioma is a rare cancer in the belly that is hard to find and hard to treat well. Researchers closely studied cancer cells from two people with this disease using detailed gene tests. These tests looked at all the genes in the cancer cells and how those genes were turned on or off. The gene results were then shared with doctors to help guide each person’s treatment plan. Later, the team checked how well the treatments worked and compared this with the gene changes they had seen. Several known cancer gene changes were found in these tumors, which may help explain how the cancer grows. Both patients’ cancer cells also showed signs that a certain growth signal path was turned on. One patient’s cancer had many more gene changes than usual, 434 compared with 18, and this person did better than expected. These findings add new knowledge about how this rare belly cancer starts and behaves over time. They may help doctors design better tests and more personal treatment plans in the future for people with this cancer.
Full-Text Summary: Peritoneal mesothelioma is a rare cancer that starts in the lining of the belly area and nearby organs. Researchers closely studied two women with this cancer to look for gene changes in their tumor cells. They used detailed lab tests on tumor samples and blood to read all the DNA in the cancer cells. Both women had changes in genes that normally act as brakes on cell growth, which may help the cancer grow. In both cases, a growth signal called MET was very active, which may be driving cancer cell growth. One woman had only 18 single-letter DNA changes in her tumor and had fast disease growth and poor response to treatment. The other woman had 434 such changes, had a strong response to chemotherapy, and was well 14 months later. This large number of changes is called a “hypermutated” pattern and may be linked to better treatment response. These findings suggest that the number and type of gene changes may help predict how this cancer behaves. In the future, detailed gene testing may help guide drug choices and surgery plans for people with this rare cancer.

Title: Response to angiotensin blockade with irbesartan in a patient with metastatic colorectal cancer
Abstract Summary: A person with advanced colon cancer had tumors that spread and did not respond to usual drugs or radiation. The cancer also caused strong side effects from standard care, so other treatment ideas were needed. Researchers read all the genetic code from one of the spreading tumors. They looked for gene changes and gene activity that might point to a new drug target. The tumor showed very high activity in a group of genes that can drive cell growth. This pattern suggested that blocking a body system that controls blood pressure might also slow the cancer. Researchers chose a common blood pressure drug called irbesartan and used it as a cancer treatment. After starting irbesartan, the person had a very strong and long-lasting tumor shrinkage. This case shows that deep genetic testing can sometimes reveal new drug uses for one person’s cancer. In the future, such testing may help doctors match some patients to unexpected, more personal treatment options.
Full-Text Summary: A woman with advanced colon cancer had tumors that kept coming back after surgery, chemo, and radiation. Doctors took a sample of her tumor and read all of its DNA and active genes in great detail. They found many gene changes and very high activity in two genes that help cancer cells grow and survive. These genes are part of a chain of signals in the cell that can be turned down by a blood pressure drug. Researchers chose the drug irbesartan, which blocks this signal chain and has shown cancer blocking effects in lab work. She started taking 150 milligrams of irbesartan by mouth each day in December 2014. Before treatment, a blood test for tumor marker was 18, which was higher than the normal limit of 5. After five weeks on irbesartan, this marker dropped to 3.1, which is in the normal range. Scans also showed that signs of active cancer almost completely went away and stayed gone for at least 10 months. This case suggests that reading the full cancer DNA and active genes can sometimes point to useful older drugs. With more careful testing, this type of gene based matching might help some people with hard to treat cancers.

Title: Sex differences in oncogenic mutational processes
Abstract Summary: Cancer can act in different ways in men and women, even outside sex organs like the breast or prostate. Researchers studied the full set of genes in 1,983 tumors from 28 cancer types. They looked for links between sex and gene changes that drive cancer growth. They checked both parts of genes that make proteins and parts that do not make proteins. They found several clear differences between men and women in these cancer gene changes. Some cancer driving changes were more common in one sex than the other. They also saw sex differences in how often certain gene changes appeared in tumors. Patterns of damage in DNA, called mutation signs, also differed between men and women. These results show that sex based molecular differences in cancer are wide spread and important. Paying closer attention to sex in cancer lab work may improve how cancers are understood and treated in the future.
Full-Text Summary: Cancer often behaves differently in men and women, even when it does not involve sex organs. Researchers studied the full DNA from 1,983 tumours from 28 cancer types in men and women. They looked for sex differences in many kinds of DNA changes, including both “important” genes and the large spaces between them. Some key cancer genes were changed more often in tumours from men, such as in liver and thyroid cancers. Across all cancers, tumours from men usually had more DNA mutations than tumours from women. In liver and kidney cancers, this higher mutation load in men was seen in both gene and non‑gene regions. Tumours from men and women also showed different patterns of larger DNA gains and losses, and these patterns varied by cancer type. Certain kinds of mutation “signatures,” which hint at how damage happens, were more common in one sex than the other. These findings suggest that cancer in men and women can grow and change in different ways at the DNA level. In the future, this type of work may help guide sex‑aware cancer research and treatment choices.

Title: Retrospective evaluation of whole exome and genome mutation calls in 746 cancer samples
Abstract Summary: Cancer cells often carry many DNA changes that help them grow and spread. Researchers compared two major DNA scan methods that read either the whole genome or only the parts that make proteins. They looked at 746 cancer samples and checked how often the two methods found the same DNA changes. About 80% of the DNA changes in protein‑making regions were found by both methods. The whole genome method found about half again as many changes in these regions as the smaller scan. It also found extra changes in hard‑to‑read DNA areas that the smaller scan often missed. Some changes were seen only by one method because the cancer cells were mixed and not all had the same change. Other changes were missed because only one computer tool picked them up in earlier work. These results show that each DNA scan has limits, even when both are done carefully and in the same cancers. The work may guide doctors and labs when they choose which DNA test to use for cancer care in the future.
Full-Text Summary: Cancer cells often carry many DNA changes, called mutations, that can be read in different ways. Researchers compared two common lab methods that read cancer DNA: one that scans only genes and one that scans the whole genome. They looked at 746 tumor samples and checked how often the two methods agreed on the same mutations. About 80 out of 100 gene-area mutations were found by both methods, showing strong agreement where coverage was good. Around 90 out of 100 samples had at least 80 percent of their gene mutations matched between the two methods. Most differences came from mutations that were rare within the tumor, choices about which calls to filter out, and some technical limits. The whole genome method also found about 700 extra mutations in known cancer genes, often in hard-to-read DNA regions. These results suggest both methods are reliable for many cancer questions, but each can miss some important changes. As whole genome tests become cheaper, they may help doctors see more of the cancer DNA picture in each patient.

Title: Integrated Analysis of Copy Number Variation, Microsatellite Instability, and Tumor Mutation Burden Identifies an 11-Gene Signature Predicting Survival in Breast Cancer
Abstract Summary: People with breast cancer can have different gene changes that affect how their disease behaves and responds to care. Researchers used large cancer data sets to study three kinds of gene changes in breast tumors. They grouped patients into two main groups based on these gene changes in their tumors. The two groups had clear differences in survival, gene changes, and the mix of immune cells around the tumor. One group had a worse outlook and fewer gene changes of a certain type linked to many mutations. From these groups, researchers found 130 genes that were turned on or off in different ways. They then built a risk score based on 11 of these genes to predict patient outlook. They checked how well this 11‑gene score could predict outcomes using standard math tests. They also tested the score in a second, separate group of breast cancer patients. The 11‑gene score showed strong promise for telling which patients might do better or worse over time. In the future, this type of gene‑based risk score might help doctors plan more personal care for breast cancer.
Full-Text Summary: Breast cancer is very common and can be deadly, especially when it has spread in the body. Researchers studied over 1,000 breast tumors to see how certain gene changes link to patient survival. They grouped the tumors into two gene types and compared stages of cancer and patient deaths. One group had more advanced cancers and more deaths, showing a clearly worse outlook over time. This group also had fewer gene changes of a certain kind, called mutation burden, than the better-outcome group. Researchers then looked at 130 genes that differed between the two groups and picked 11 linked to survival. They built a risk score using these 11 genes and split patients into high and low risk groups. People in the high risk group died more often, and the score predicted 1, 3, and 5 year survival well. The score also worked in a second group of 50 breast cancer patients from another database. A chart that combines this gene score with basic clinical facts may help doctors estimate a person’s outlook. If confirmed in more patients, this kind of gene-based risk tool could guide follow-up and treatment choices.

Title: The impact of whole genome and transcriptome analysis (WGTA) on predictive biomarker discovery and diagnostic accuracy of advanced malignancies
Abstract Summary: People with advanced cancer often need better tests to guide treatment and confirm where the cancer started. Researchers used a broad DNA and gene activity test on 652 cancer samples from many body sites. They made reports that listed key gene changes and also predicted the body site where each cancer began. Two cancer experts then reviewed these reports along with medical history and lab slides from the tumors. In most cases, the cancer type from this new test matched the earlier lab diagnosis, about 94 out of 100 cases. In a few cases, the new test led to a change in the cancer type or did not add clear help. All 15 cancers that were hard to name before were given a clear cancer type by this test. The test also found gene changes linked to approved targeted drugs in 39 cases, about 6 percent. Using newer drug rules from 2021, that number rose to 103 cases, about 16 percent. This kind of broad gene test may help doctors choose drugs and better tell where a cancer started. Work is now aimed at making this test cheaper and more useful for everyday cancer care.
Full-Text Summary: Cancer doctors often need to know exactly where a tumor started and which drugs might work best. Researchers used a very detailed gene test, called whole genome and transcriptome analysis, on 652 people with advanced cancer. They compared these gene results with usual lab tests and medical records to check cancer type and drug options. At the time of testing, this deep gene test found drug targets already linked to approved treatments in 39 people, or 6%. Using newer 2021 treatment rules, that number rose to 103 people, or 16%. In 389 cancers checked, the gene test agreed with the original diagnosis in 94% of cases. In 15 people where doctors could not tell where the cancer started, the gene test was able to name a likely cancer type every time. These new answers were used to guide more tests, treatment plans, and talks with patients about their disease. These results suggest that broad gene testing can help confirm cancer type and uncover extra treatment options for some people with hard‑to‑treat cancers.

Title: Whole-genome and transcriptome analysis of advanced adrenocortical cancer highlights multiple alterations affecting epigenome and DNA repair pathways
Abstract Summary: Cancer of the adrenal gland, called adrenocortical cancer, is rare and often hard to treat well. Researchers studied tumor samples from seven people whose cancer had spread to other parts of the body. They read all the DNA and activity messages in these tumors to look for key gene changes. They found several main gene changes that seem to drive this cancer, but treatment choices remain very limited. Many tumors had damage in genes that control cell growth and genes that fix broken DNA. Some tumors also had changes in genes that protect the ends of chromosomes, which help cells stay stable. A test that looks for a pattern of DNA damage found that some tumors could not repair DNA well. Other tumors showed changes in genes that control how DNA is packed and read inside the cell. These weak spots in DNA repair and DNA control may be used as targets for new cancer drugs. In the future, people with this rare cancer might get lab tests to match them with more exact, gene-based treatments.
Full-Text Summary: Adrenocortical cancer is a rare cancer that starts in the adrenal gland above the kidney. Many people already have spread of the cancer when it is found, and long‑term survival is low. Usual drugs, including standard chemotherapy and a hormone‑blocking drug, often do not work well for this cancer. Researchers closely studied the DNA and gene activity of tumors from seven people with advanced disease. They looked for gene changes that drive cancer growth and for weak spots that new drugs might target. They found common damage in genes that control cell growth, DNA repair, and how DNA is packed and read in cells. Changes in several DNA repair genes suggested that four of the seven cancers had trouble fixing DNA damage. Two tumors showed a clear pattern of poor DNA repair, and one patient stayed stable for 8.5 months on a repair‑targeting drug. Some tumors also showed signs that drugs aimed at cell cycle control or certain gene‑reading proteins might help. These results suggest that careful gene testing may help match some people with this rare cancer to more tailored treatments.

Title: Identification of Neoantigens and Construction of Immune Subtypes in Prostate Adenocarcinoma
Abstract Summary: Men with prostate gland cancer need better treatment choices that can target their tumors more exactly. Researchers used large cancer data sets to look for tumor markers that could guide a new type of shot called an mRNA vaccine. They studied gene activity and health records from men with prostate gland cancer in two big public groups of patients. Seven tumor markers were linked with worse survival and with immune cells that can show tumor parts to the immune system. The seven markers may work as targets for future mRNA vaccines against prostate gland cancer. The team also found five immune types of this cancer, each with different cell and health features. Two types, called C3 and C5, had many immune cells around the tumor, but these cells were held back from fighting. Two other types, C1 and C2, had few immune cells near the tumor and may respond better to a vaccine. The full immune picture showed that patients with this cancer can be very different from each other. These results suggest that mRNA vaccines for prostate gland cancer may work best in people with C1 and C2 types.
Full-Text Summary: Prostate adenocarcinoma is a common cancer in men, and many patients still die even after standard treatment. Researchers looked for targets in prostate tumors that could be used to make a new type of cancer shot called an mRNA vaccine. They studied gene activity and changes in tumor samples from 643 men with this cancer. Seven tumor markers were linked to shorter survival and to strong contact with certain immune cells in the tumor. These seven markers may help the immune system see and attack prostate cancer cells when used in a vaccine. Researchers also grouped tumors into five immune types, called C1 to C5, based on immune gene patterns. Men with C1 and C2 tumors lived longer and had lower blood markers of aggressive disease than other groups. C1 and C2 tumors had more gene changes that may help the immune system react to an mRNA vaccine. C3 and C5 tumors showed signs of a blocked immune state, which might limit vaccine benefit. Overall, C1 and C2 patients appear to be the best candidates for future prostate mRNA vaccines.

Title: A Transcription Factor Signature Can Identify the CMS4 Subtype and Stratify the Prognostic Risk of Colorectal Cancer
Abstract Summary: Colon cancer can act in many different ways, and current group systems do not sort patients by risk very well. Researchers used large cancer gene data to build a new risk tool based on nine key control genes. They compared one hard to treat colon cancer type with other types to find gene changes linked to worse disease. They then built a network map of these genes to pick the most important ones for the risk tool. The tool was tested in two large groups of people with colon cancer, with 351 and 565 patients. People placed in the high risk group by this tool had much shorter survival than those in the low risk group. This link with poor survival stayed strong even when age and other health details were taken into account. The tool predicted outcome better than other gene tools, with a score of 0.65 versus 0.51 to 0.57. High risk tumors showed signs of a weak body defense space around the cancer, with strong shut down signals. These signs suggest many high risk patients may not gain much from some new immune drugs. This new risk tool may help doctors sort colon cancer patients and plan more personal care in the future.
Full-Text Summary: Colon cancer is common and deadly, and people with the same stage can still have very different outcomes. Researchers studied over 1,500 people with colon cancer to find gene patterns linked to higher or lower risk. They focused on one very aggressive tumor type, called CMS4, which has the worst survival among four main types. From many genes, they picked nine key “control” genes and built a risk score called TF-9. Each patient’s tumor got a TF-9 score, then people were split into high-risk and low-risk groups by the middle score. People in the high-risk group lived for a shorter time and had cancer come back more often than low-risk people. This result stayed true even when age, stage, and other clinical factors were taken into account. TF-9 predicted survival better than three other gene-based risk tools, with a higher accuracy score of 0.65. High-risk tumors showed signs of a “shut down” immune system and high levels of three immune markers. These markers suggest that common immune drugs may not work well, but other immune targets might help some patients. TF-9 may help doctors sort patients by risk and guide treatment choices more exactly in the future.

Title: Substitution mutational signatures in whole-genome-sequenced cancers in the UK population
Abstract Summary: Cancer cells carry many DNA changes, like spelling mistakes in a long book of instructions. Researchers read the full DNA code from over 12,000 people with cancer and matched normal tissue. They also compared these results with DNA data from more than 18,000 other cancers from two large groups. By looking at patterns in these DNA changes, they found 40 new common patterns and 18 new paired patterns. Each pattern, or “signature,” can point to a type of damage or repair problem in the cancer cells. In each organ, most cancers shared only a few common patterns, plus many rare patterns that showed up less often. Researchers also suggested a clear way to sort and use these common and rare patterns in later work. These patterns may help explain how a person’s cancer started and how it keeps growing. In the future, this kind of pattern reading might guide more exact tests and treatment choices for some patients.
Full-Text Summary: Cancer cells collect many DNA changes over time, like spelling mistakes in a long book of instructions. Researchers read the full DNA from over 18,000 cancers from many organs using a broad lab test called whole‑genome sequencing. They looked for repeat patterns in these DNA changes, called “signatures,” which can point to damage from things like sunlight or smoking. They studied 19 kinds of cancer, including lung, breast, bowel, brain, kidney, and blood cancers. For each organ, they found a small set of common signatures and a long list of rare ones. Across all cancers, they confirmed 42 known single‑letter patterns and 9 known double‑letter patterns. They also discovered 40 new single‑letter and 18 new double‑letter patterns that had not been seen before. Some signatures match known causes, such as tobacco smoke, ultraviolet light, certain drugs, or problems in DNA repair systems. These patterns can reveal hidden weaknesses in how a tumor repairs DNA, even when gene tests do not show a clear cause. Such repair problems may help doctors choose treatments like immune drugs or drugs that target broken repair pathways. Researchers also built a step‑by‑step computer method to help doctors and scientists spot common and rare signatures in new patients.

Title: Investigation of fatty acid metabolism-related genes in breast cancer: Implications for Immunotherapy and clinical significance
Abstract Summary: Breast cancer is a major health problem worldwide, with many deaths and few cases found at an early stage. Researchers looked at breast cancer tissue and grouped tumors by how they use certain fats for energy and growth. They used large sets of gene and health data from cancer databases to sort these tumors into types. Two clear types were found, each with a different mix of immune cells and a different outlook for patients. One type was linked to better chances of survival, while the other type was linked to worse outcomes. Researchers then built a risk score that adds up the effect of several fat use genes in each tumor. They checked this score in more than one large patient group to see if it could predict outcomes. The risk score may help guide choices about chemo drugs and new immune based drugs for breast cancer. A simple chart tool was also made to help doctors use the risk score in daily care. These results suggest that measuring how breast tumors use fats could help match patients with better treatment plans.
Full-Text Summary: Breast cancer is very common and still causes many deaths, even with better surgery, drugs, and radiation. Researchers looked at genes that help the body handle fats, to see how changes in these genes link to breast cancer. They studied 471 fat‑related genes in over 1,000 women with breast cancer and compared them with normal breast tissue. Many of these genes had changes in their DNA, and about 16% of patients showed such changes in this gene group. Two main breast cancer groups were found, based on fat‑related genes, and one group lived longer than the other. These two groups also had different immune cell patterns and different chances of responding to immune and chemo drugs. One gene, called FABP4, seemed to protect against tumors early, but later could help cancer grow over time. A risk score using seven fat‑related genes was built to sort patients into high‑ and low‑risk groups. People with a low risk score lived longer and often had better predicted response to some treatments. This risk score could help doctors estimate survival and choose immune or chemo drugs more wisely for breast cancer.

Title: Multiple m6A RNA methylation modulators promote the malignant progression of hepatocellular carcinoma and affect its clinical prognosis
Abstract Summary: Liver cancer called hepatocellular carcinoma is a major cause of cancer death around the world. Researchers looked at tiny chemical marks on cell messages in liver cancer and in normal liver tissue. They used large public cancer data sets to compare levels of 13 of these message mark proteins in the samples. Twelve of the 13 proteins showed clear differences between liver cancer tissue and normal liver tissue. Researchers then split the liver cancer samples into two groups based on these protein levels. People in group two had shorter life, more advanced cancer stage, and worse tumor grade. Researchers built a risk score using four of the message mark proteins that linked to patient survival. This risk score also matched how advanced the cancer was and worked as an independent sign of outcome. These results suggest these message mark proteins help drive liver cancer growth and spread. They may help doctors better predict how a person with liver cancer will do and guide treatment choices in the future.
Full-Text Summary: Liver cancer of the main liver cells is a leading cause of cancer death worldwide. Researchers studied tiny chemical marks on cell messages, called “methyl” marks, that can change how cells grow and divide. They looked at 13 genes that control these marks in hundreds of liver cancer and normal liver samples from large databases. Twelve of the 13 genes showed different activity levels in cancer tissue compared with normal tissue. Cancer samples were split into two groups based on these gene patterns, called cluster 1 and cluster 2. People in cluster 2 had more advanced cancer, worse tumor grade, and shorter overall survival time. Four of the genes were used to build a “risk score” that grouped patients into high and low risk. People with a high risk score had more advanced stage, worse tumor grade, and shorter survival than low risk people. The risk score stayed useful for predicting survival even after considering age, sex, and cancer stage. These results suggest that these gene changes may help guide future liver cancer prognosis and treatment choices.

Title: Loss of CDH16 expression is a strong independent predictor for lymph node metastasis in Middle Eastern papillary thyroid cancer
Abstract Summary: Papillary thyroid cancer is the most common type of cancer that starts in the thyroid gland in the neck. Researchers looked at a protein called CDH16, which helps thyroid cells stick together and form normal thyroid parts. They tested 1606 thyroid cancer samples and 240 normal thyroid samples to measure how much CDH16 was present. CDH16 was seen in all normal thyroid samples, but in only about 9 out of 100 cancer samples. Loss of CDH16 was linked with more serious cancer signs, like spread to both sides of the thyroid. It was also linked with cancer spread to neck lymph nodes and to other body parts. People whose tumors lacked CDH16 were more likely to have certain gene changes tied to thyroid cancer. Lack of CDH16 made lymph node spread about two and a half times more likely, even after other factors were checked. People without CDH16 in their tumors had a shorter time without the cancer coming back. CDH16 testing may help doctors tell which thyroid cancers are more risky and need closer care. In the future, drugs that raise CDH16 levels might help treat some thyroid cancers.
Full-Text Summary: Papillary thyroid cancer is the most common thyroid cancer and is becoming more common worldwide. Researchers studied a protein called CDH16, which helps thyroid cells stick together and stay organized. They tested 240 normal thyroid samples and 1,606 papillary thyroid cancer samples from people in Saudi Arabia. CDH16 was present in all normal thyroid samples but in only about 9 out of 100 cancer samples. Cancers that had lost CDH16 were more likely to be in both thyroid lobes and in many spots. These cancers were also more likely to grow outside the thyroid and spread to lymph nodes and distant organs. Loss of CDH16 made spread to lymph nodes about two and a half times more likely, even after other factors were checked. People whose tumors lacked CDH16 had cancer come back sooner than those whose tumors still had it. The shortest time without cancer was seen when CDH16 loss occurred together with a change in another gene called TERT. CDH16 testing on tumor samples may help doctors judge how aggressive a papillary thyroid cancer is and plan follow-up care.

Title: The Mutographs biorepository: A unique genomic resource to study cancer around the world
Abstract Summary: Cancer can start for many reasons, and these reasons can differ between people and countries. Researchers collected over 7,800 cancer samples from people in 30 countries on five continents. They also gathered details about age, sex, daily habits, where people live, and their medical care. Deep gene testing is being finished for over 4,000 of these cancer samples. The main goal is to learn what causes cancer in eight different parts of the body. All the gene, exposure, and medical data will be shared on a large open website for cancer research. This shared data can help experts study how the world around us and our genes work together in cancer. Large shared banks of samples and data are key for better cancer prevention, early finding, and treatment. The project will also support many new team projects across the world in the future. Over time, this work may guide safer habits, better screening tests, and more exact care for people with cancer.
Full-Text Summary: Cancer rates differ a lot between countries, and genes alone do not explain these gaps. Many cases likely come from things people are exposed to, such as tobacco, alcohol, diet, or hot drinks. Researchers built a large shared bank of cancer samples and health data from 7,808 people in 30 countries. They focused on eight cancers, including those of the food pipe, kidney, bowel, pancreas, stomach area, head and neck, bladder, and gallbladder. They collected tumor tissue, blood, and detailed information on habits like smoking, drinking, hot drinks, and certain local products such as opium or maté tea. Over 4,000 cases already have full DNA reading of both tumor and normal cells. Early work in food pipe cancer found clear DNA damage patterns linked to opium and alcohol use. The project includes many people from regions that were rarely part of past genetic cancer research. These data will be shared worldwide so many teams can search for new causes of cancer and better ways to prevent it. Over time, this may help shape safer lifestyle advice and public health rules in different parts of the world.

Title: PLK1 and FoxM1 expressions positively correlate in papillary thyroid carcinoma and their combined inhibition results in synergistic anti-tumor effects
Abstract Summary: Papillary thyroid cancer is a common thyroid cancer that can sometimes grow and spread faster than expected. Researchers looked at a cell control protein called PLK1 in many thyroid cancer samples and lab models. They found that over half, about 54 percent, of these cancers had high levels of PLK1. Cancers with more PLK1 were linked with more aggressive features and came back sooner after treatment. PLK1 helps cancer cells divide, stay alive, and keep making new cells. When researchers blocked PLK1 in thyroid cancer cells, the cells stopped dividing and many died. Blocking PLK1 also reduced the cancer cells’ ability to form new cell clusters, which can act like seeds. PLK1 works closely with another control protein called FoxM1, and they can bind to each other. Lowering PLK1 levels also lowered FoxM1 levels, which suggests PLK1 acts through this partner. Using two drugs together, one blocking PLK1 and one blocking FoxM1, slowed cancer cell growth more than either alone. In animal tests, this drug pair also delayed tumor growth. These results suggest that testing PLK1 levels may help predict which thyroid cancers act more aggressively. In the future, drugs that block both PLK1 and FoxM1 might offer a new option for hard-to-treat thyroid cancer.
Full-Text Summary: Papillary thyroid cancer is the most common type of thyroid cancer and can sometimes come back or spread. Researchers studied a protein called PLK1, which helps cells grow and divide, in over 1,600 thyroid cancer samples. They found high PLK1 levels in about 54% of these cancers, and these tumors were more aggressive. High PLK1 was linked with spread to neck lymph nodes and a higher chance of the cancer returning. People with high PLK1 had shorter time without the cancer coming back, even after other factors were considered. In lab tests, blocking PLK1 slowed cancer cell growth and caused cancer cells to die. Blocking PLK1 also reduced the ability of cancer cells to form tight clumps, which can act like “seed” cells for new tumors. PLK1 worked closely with another protein, FoxM1, and both were often high in the same tumors. When drugs that block PLK1 and FoxM1 were given together, cancer cell growth dropped more than with either drug alone. In mice with thyroid tumors, this drug pair made tumors grow more slowly without clear weight loss. These results suggest that testing PLK1 levels may help predict which thyroid cancers act more aggressively. Blocking PLK1, especially together with FoxM1, may become a future treatment option for some patients.

Title: Exploration of Germline Correlates and Risk of Immune-Related Adverse Events in Advanced Cancer Patients Treated with Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors
Abstract Summary: Many people with cancer now get a type of drug called an immune checkpoint blocker, which helps the immune system fight tumors. These drugs can also cause the immune system to attack healthy organs, leading to serious side effects in some people. Researchers looked at 117 people with advanced cancers who got these drugs as part of their care. They checked medical charts to see who had immune side effects, such as liver or lung problems. They also studied each person’s genes using blood and tumor samples taken at the same time. A group of gene types, called HLA-B27, was linked to bad liver and lung side effects in some patients. These side effects were more common when people got certain drug pairs that boost the immune system strongly. The link was strong enough that it was unlikely to be due to chance alone. The results suggest that some people may be born with genes that raise their risk of these immune side effects. In the future, gene tests might help doctors spot people who need closer watching or different drug plans.
Full-Text Summary: Immune checkpoint drugs help the immune system attack many types of cancer, but they can also harm healthy organs. These harmful effects are called immune‑related side effects and can affect the skin, gut, glands, lungs, and liver. Researchers looked at 117 adults with advanced cancer who got these drugs and had their blood and tumor genes tested. About half of the patients, 60 out of 117, had some kind of immune‑related side effect. Most side effects were mild skin rashes, gut problems like diarrhea, or hormone problems like low thyroid levels. Seven patients, or about 6 percent, had severe side effects, mainly serious liver or lung inflammation. People getting two immune drugs together had side effects more often than people getting a single drug. Patients who already had an autoimmune disease were more likely to have side effects, sometimes worse ones. The team also checked inherited genes that guide how the immune system works. They found one gene type, called HLA‑B27, in 6 patients, and 4 of these had severe liver or lung problems. In people without this gene type, only about 3 percent had severe side effects. These results suggest that some people may be born with a higher risk of strong immune side effects. In the future, simple blood gene tests might help doctors choose immune drugs and watch some patients more closely.

Title: Geographic variation of mutagenic exposures in kidney cancer genomes
Abstract Summary: Kidney cancer rates differ a lot between countries, and known risks like smoking and obesity do not fully explain this gap. Researchers studied 962 kidney tumors from 11 countries with different cancer rates and read all their DNA changes. They compared the patterns of these DNA changes between countries to look for signs of different harmful exposures. The patterns of DNA changes were not the same in each country, showing country specific cancer causes. In Romania, Serbia, and Thailand, most tumors showed a pattern linked to a plant poison called aristolochic acid. This poison pattern was rare in tumors from other countries, suggesting different local risks. In Japan, over 70% of tumors shared another clear DNA pattern, but this pattern was almost absent elsewhere. One more common DNA pattern was seen in all countries, but it was stronger where kidney cancer rates were higher. DNA patterns linked to smoking matched how much people smoked in each country, but not obesity or high blood pressure. This means some risks may cause cancer in ways that do not leave clear DNA damage marks. Overall, the work points to several unknown, place based cancer causes that may affect many millions of people worldwide.
Full-Text Summary: Kidney cancer called clear cell type is common in many countries, but rates differ a lot between places. Researchers studied 962 people with this kidney cancer from 11 countries across Europe, Asia, and the Americas. They read the full DNA code of each tumor and compared the patterns of damage between countries. Some countries, like Romania, Serbia, and Thailand, showed DNA damage linked to plant poisons called aristolochic acids. In these places, this pattern appeared in most tumors, suggesting many people were exposed to these plant toxins. In Japan, a different, unknown type of DNA damage pattern appeared in over 70% of kidney cancers. Another common damage pattern, also from an unknown cause, was stronger in countries with higher kidney cancer rates. This pattern was tied to signs of poor kidney function in blood, hinting at a harmful exposure or kidney stress. Smoking-related DNA damage matched how much people smoked, but no clear DNA pattern linked to obesity or high blood pressure. These results suggest some cancer risks act by directly damaging DNA, while others may work in different ways. Future work may find the sources of these hidden exposures, which could guide public health steps to lower kidney cancer risk.

Title: Predicting factors and clinical outcome of biochemical incomplete response in middle eastern differentiated thyroid carcinoma
Abstract Summary: People with a common type of thyroid cancer can have blood test changes after treatment, even when scans look clear. Researchers looked back at 1,286 people from the Middle East who had thyroid surgery and radiation treatment. They checked which basic health and tumor features were linked to these blood test changes after treatment. About one in five people, 266 out of 1,286, had these blood changes over about ten years of follow up. Higher cancer blood levels before radiation, cancer in neck nodes, being male, and delayed radiation raised the chance. Among the 266 people with blood changes, about 37 out of 100 later showed clear cancer on scans. Being male and having rising cancer blood levels after treatment made this risk even higher. People who had both of these risks had worse time without signs of cancer coming back. Simple facts, like timing of treatment and early blood test levels, may help doctors spot higher risk people sooner. People with these signs may need closer follow up and care plans that fit their personal level of risk.
Full-Text Summary: People with a common type of thyroid cancer often do well, but some still have signs of cancer in blood tests. Researchers looked at 1,286 people from the Middle East who had thyroid surgery and radioactive iodine treatment. They checked how many had ongoing abnormal blood tests, called a “biochemical incomplete response,” after first treatment. About 1 in 5 patients, or 20.7%, had this kind of incomplete response over about 10 years of follow-up. Men, people with cancer in neck lymph nodes, and those who got iodine treatment after three months had higher risk. A higher level of a cancer blood marker before iodine treatment also strongly linked to this incomplete response. Among the 266 people with incomplete response, about 37% later showed clear cancer on scans or exams. In these patients, being male and having rising blood marker levels over time meant higher chance of visible cancer. People with both of these risk factors had much lower chances of staying free of cancer over 10 years. These results suggest some patients may need closer checkups and more tailored care after thyroid cancer treatment.

Title: Radioactive iodine refractoriness in Middle Eastern differentiated thyroid cancer: clinical outcome and risk factor analysis
Abstract Summary: People with a certain type of thyroid cancer sometimes stop responding to standard radioactive iodine treatment. Some of these people live many years, while others do not, and doctors want to understand why. Researchers looked back at records from 268 people treated at one medical center. They checked who had cancer spread, who had gene changes, and how long people lived from thyroid cancer. About 37 out of 100 people had cancer that spread to distant body parts, like lungs or bones. People older than 45 years had a higher chance of dying from thyroid cancer than younger people. People whose cancer had spread to other body parts also had worse survival. A certain gene change in the cancer, called a TERT change, was linked with shorter life. People were placed into low, middle, or high risk groups based on these three factors. After ten years, survival was 100% in low risk, about 93% in middle risk, and about 54% in high risk. Knowing these risk signs may help doctors plan closer follow up and stronger treatment for those at higher risk.
Full-Text Summary: Some thyroid cancers stop taking up a common treatment called radioactive iodine, which makes them harder to treat well. Researchers reviewed records from 268 people with this type of thyroid cancer treated at one hospital in Saudi Arabia. They looked at age, spread of cancer, and certain gene changes to see which were linked to death from thyroid cancer. People 45 years or older had a much higher risk of dying from their thyroid cancer than younger people. Cancer that had spread to distant body parts, like the lungs or bones, also raised the risk of death. A change in a gene that controls how cells keep their DNA ends, called a TERT change, raised risk as well. When none of these three risk factors were present, 10-year survival was 100 percent. With one or two risk factors, 10-year survival was about 93 percent, and with all three, about 54 percent. These risk groups may help doctors decide who needs closer follow-up and stronger treatment and who may not. In the future, this kind of risk sorting could guide more personal care plans for people with this thyroid cancer.

Title: The Prognostic Impact of Tumor Size and BRAF Mutational Status in Middle Eastern Differentiated Thyroid Cancer
Abstract Summary: People with thyroid cancer often ask if the size of the tumor at diagnosis affects their future health. Researchers looked at 1,709 people from the Middle East who had thyroid cancer surgery. They grouped people by tumor size and by whether the cancer had a certain gene change or not. They then compared how long people stayed free from cancer coming back or getting worse. Tumors larger than 4 centimeters were linked with older age, being male, and more spread of cancer in the neck. Larger tumors were also linked with more cases of cancer coming back or not going away. Tumor size and the gene change each seemed linked with how long people stayed free of cancer events. When groups were studied more closely, larger tumors predicted worse outcomes, even without the gene change. Among people whose tumors did have the gene change, larger tumors still predicted worse outcomes. Overall, tumor size at diagnosis gave important information about future risk, no matter the gene change status. These results may help doctors use tumor size to guide follow up plans and treatment choices for thyroid cancer.
Full-Text Summary: People with thyroid cancer often live many years, but some have cancer that comes back or does not go away. The research focused on whether the size of the thyroid tumor at diagnosis helps predict these later problems. Researchers looked back at 1,709 people in the Middle East who had surgery for thyroid cancer. They grouped people by tumor size, using 4 centimeters as the cut point for small versus large tumors. About one in five people had tumors larger than 4 centimeters at diagnosis. Larger tumors were linked with older age, more men, and cancer spread outside the thyroid. Larger tumors were also tied to more cases where cancer stayed or came back after treatment. A common gene change in thyroid cancer was checked, but tumor size still predicted outcome on its own. People with larger tumors had shorter times without cancer coming back, no matter their gene change status. This means tumor size alone can help doctors judge risk in Middle Eastern thyroid cancer patients. In the future, tumor size at diagnosis may guide how closely patients are watched after treatment.

Title: KRAS inhibitors may prevent colorectal cancer metachronous metastasis by suppressing TGF‑β mediated epithelial‑mesenchymal transition
Abstract Summary: People with colon or rectal cancer sometimes later grow new tumors in other body parts, called metachronous spread. Some of these cancers have a certain gene change that seems to raise the chance of this later spread. Researchers used large public data sets to test if this gene change was linked to higher spread risk. They then built a risk score with computer tools to predict which people with this gene change are high risk. In lab tests, drug blockers of this gene change made high risk cancer cells move and invade much less. These drug effects were also seen in tiny tumor samples and in mice with cancer spread to the liver. More tests showed the drugs slowed a process that lets cancer cells loosen, move, and travel in the body. Adding a certain signal protein partly removed the good effect of the drugs on the cancer cells. Overall, the work suggests these drugs might help stop later spread in people with this gene change. In the future, such drugs might be used early in high risk patients to lower the chance of new tumors.
Full-Text Summary: Colon cancer can come back in other body parts months or years after surgery, called metachronous metastasis. Many people with colon cancer have a change in a gene called KRAS, and this change is very common. Researchers checked data from past patients and found that KRAS changes raised the risk of later spread after surgery. They built a risk score using 36 genes to sort people with KRAS changes into high‑risk and low‑risk groups. People in the high‑risk group had more cancer spread after surgery than those in the low‑risk group. Researchers then tested new drugs that block KRAS in colon cancer cells and in mice. These KRAS‑blocking drugs made cancer cells move and invade less, and reduced liver spread in mice. The drugs seemed to calm a process that lets cancer cells loosen and travel, driven by a signal called TGF‑beta. Adding extra TGF‑beta partly removed the good effect of the KRAS‑blocking drugs on cell movement. Longer drug use could still lower cancer cell movement, even when cells became less sensitive to the drug. These results suggest KRAS‑blocking drugs might one day help stop high‑risk colon cancers from spreading again after surgery.

Title: The complexity of tobacco smoke-induced mutagenesis in head and neck cancer
Abstract Summary: Head and neck cancer often starts because of tobacco smoke, and the risk is even higher when people also drink alcohol. Researchers studied cancer DNA from 265 people with head and neck cancer from eight different countries. They looked for patterns of gene damage linked to tobacco and found six clear tobacco damage patterns. Some of these damage patterns had not been seen before in this type of cancer. Countries with more head and neck cancer also had more tobacco‑type DNA damage in these tumors. Different parts of the head and neck showed different levels of tobacco‑linked DNA damage. This means some tissues may get hurt more easily by smoke than others. Tobacco smoke and alcohol together left a special mix of damage patterns in the cancer DNA. Tobacco use was tied to changes in key cancer genes and in the number of gene copies in cells. These results show that tobacco smoke can push cancer cells to grow and change in many ways. This work supports strong efforts to prevent and stop tobacco and heavy alcohol use to lower cancer risk.
Full-Text Summary: Head and neck cancer includes cancers of the mouth, throat, and voice box and is often linked to smoking and drinking. Researchers studied DNA from 265 head and neck cancers from people in eight countries with different smoking and drinking habits. They read the full DNA code of each tumor and compared it with blood from the same person. Cancers from people who smoked had more DNA changes than cancers from people who never smoked. Several clear patterns of DNA damage were tied to tobacco, and one new pattern was seen mostly in mouth cancers. Usual tobacco damage patterns were much more common in voice box cancers than in other head and neck sites. Alcohol alone caused fewer cancers, but drinking plus smoking led to special damage patterns and many changes in an important control gene. In many cases, most DNA changes could not be linked to smoking, drinking, or virus infection, suggesting other unknown causes. These results support efforts to prevent head and neck cancer by cutting tobacco use and limiting alcohol, especially together.

Title: Geographic and age variations in mutational processes in colorectal cancer
Abstract Summary: Colon cancer rates are different in many parts of the world and have changed over time. In many countries, colon cancer in people under age 50 has about doubled in twenty years. The reasons for this rise are not yet known. Researchers studied the full cancer DNA from 981 people with colon cancer in 11 countries. They saw no big DNA pattern changes in one special cancer type, but saw changes in the others. Several DNA change patterns were more common in some countries, showing different harmful exposures in those places. Two patterns came from a poison made by certain gut bacteria, called colibactin. These two patterns were stronger in countries that had more colon cancer cases. They were also 3.3 times more common in people under 40 than in people over 70. These bacteria linked to early DNA damage in a key cancer control gene. About one quarter of certain gene breaks in these cases came from this bacteria poison pattern. The work suggests that contact with these bacteria early in life may raise colon cancer risk at a young age.
Full-Text Summary: Colon cancer and rectal cancer together are called colorectal cancer, and rates differ a lot between countries. Researchers read the full DNA code of 981 colorectal cancers from 11 countries and compared age groups and locations. They focused on 802 cancers with working DNA repair, since these better show outside damage over time. They looked for “signatures,” which are patterns of DNA damage that point to certain harmful exposures, like a fingerprint. Some signatures were more common in certain countries, suggesting different environmental or lifestyle exposures in those places. One key finding involved a poison made by some gut bacteria, called colibactin, which leaves a clear damage pattern in DNA. Cancers with this colibactin pattern were found more often in countries with higher colorectal cancer rates, especially in the rectum. These colibactin patterns were also much more common in people under 50, and even more in those under 40. The damage seemed to happen early in life and was linked to important gene changes that can start cancer growth. These results suggest that early-life contact with certain gut bacteria may raise the chance of colorectal cancer at a younger age. Future work may test if lowering or blocking these bacteria in early life can help prevent some cancers.

Title: Decoding Senescence‐Driven Heterogeneity in Early‐Onset Colorectal Cancer for Prognostic and Therapeutic Stratification
Abstract Summary: Some people under age 50 get colon or rectal cancer that grows fast and is hard to treat. Researchers studied almost 3,000 people with this early cancer to look at how old or “tired” the tumor cells seemed. They found that these “tired” cell features were stronger and more mixed in younger patients, and did not match real age. Two main groups of tumors appeared based on this cell aging pattern. One group had less cell aging, people lived longer, and their immune system seemed more active against the cancer. The other group had more cell aging, more aggressive tumors, and a weaker immune response around the tumor. Researchers then built a score, called EO-Senscore, to measure how much cell aging each tumor had. This score helped sort patients into groups with different chances of doing well and different likely treatment responses. People with a low score were more likely to benefit from standard drugs and immune based treatment. People with a high score had more invasive tumors but their cancer cells were sensitive to special “senolytic” drugs in lab tests. This work shows that cell aging is a key part of why this cancer can be so aggressive. The score may help doctors choose between immune drugs, usual drugs, or new drug mixes for more tailored care in the future.
Full-Text Summary: Colon and rectal cancer in people under age 50 is rising and often acts more aggressive than in older adults. Researchers studied nearly 3,000 people with this cancer to look at a process called cell aging inside tumor cells. They found that younger patients’ tumors showed stronger signs of cell aging, even though the patients themselves were not old. Two main tumor groups appeared. One group had lower cell aging, fewer spread signs, and people lived longer after treatment. The other group had higher cell aging, more spread to lymph nodes and distant sites, and worse survival. Researchers then built a score, called EO‑Senscore, based on tumor lab tests to measure this cell aging level. People with a low score tended to do better and were more likely to respond to immune‑based and standard drugs. People with a high score had more invasive tumors but their cancer cells were more sensitive to a drug that kills aged cells. These results suggest the score might help match younger colon cancer patients to the treatments most likely to help them. Further trials are needed before this tool can guide everyday care in clinics.

Title: Observational study on the safety and effectiveness of SARS-CoV-2 vaccination in patients with lung cancer
Abstract Summary: People with lung cancer face high risk from the virus that causes COVID-19. Researchers in Spain looked at adults with lung cancer who got a COVID-19 shot between 2021 and early 2022. All had lung cancer of any type or stage and got a vaccine approved in Europe at that time. They followed these people for three months after the shot to see safety and infections. There were 794 people in the group, most were men, and the average age was 66 years. About three out of four people received three doses of vaccine. About three in ten people had side effects from the vaccine, but very few were severe. Only one person had a very serious vaccine side effect, and none had the most extreme level. Side effects from cancer treatment were a bit more common, and some were very serious, but none were fatal. After vaccination, 58 people, or about 7 in 100, caught the virus. Of those infected, 10 needed hospital care, but none needed intensive care or died. Overall, the vaccines helped protect many people with lung cancer and kept illness milder when infection happened. These results support using COVID-19 vaccines to help protect people living with lung cancer.
Full-Text Summary: People with lung cancer have a higher chance of dying from COVID‑19 than people without cancer. Researchers followed 794 adults with lung cancer in Spain who got COVID‑19 vaccines between 2021 and 2022. Most people got three doses of vaccine, mainly the two most common brands used in Europe. About 30% had side effects from the vaccine, usually mild problems like tiredness, fever, or arm pain. Only one person had a very serious vaccine side effect, and no one died from the vaccine. Side effects from cancer treatment after vaccination were also common but stayed within usual, expected levels. After vaccination, 58 people, or about 7%, caught COVID‑19 during follow‑up. Only 10 of these 58 people needed to stay in the hospital, and none needed intensive care. No one died from COVID‑19 after getting the vaccine, even among those who were hospitalised. Overall, the chance of getting COVID‑19 within nine months after the first dose was about 5%. Getting COVID‑19 before or after vaccination did not shorten overall survival in this group. These results suggest COVID‑19 vaccines are safe and give useful protection for many people with lung cancer.

Title: Comparison of MAPIE versus MAP in patients with a poor response to preoperative chemotherapy for newly diagnosed high-grade osteosarcoma (EURAMOS-1): an open-label, international, randomised controlled trial
Abstract Summary: Osteosarcoma is a fast growing bone cancer that often affects children, teens, and young adults up to age 40. Researchers wanted to know if stronger chemo after surgery could help people whose tumors did not shrink well before surgery. They compared a standard chemo mix after surgery with a stronger mix that added two more chemo drugs. Over six years, 618 people with a poor tumor response were split into the two treatment groups by chance. About half of the people in each group had the cancer come back, grow, or cause death during follow up. There was almost no difference in the time people stayed free of these cancer problems between the two groups. The stronger chemo did not help people live longer without cancer events compared with the standard chemo. The stronger chemo caused more serious side effects, such as very low blood counts and other organ problems. Because of this, the standard chemo mix after surgery remains the usual treatment for this group of patients. New treatment ideas are needed to better help people whose bone tumors do not respond well to first chemo.
Full-Text Summary: Osteosarcoma is a rare bone cancer that often affects children and young adults and can be deadly. Doctors usually treat it with strong cancer drugs, then surgery to remove the bone tumor, then more drugs. Some patients’ tumors do not shrink well with the first round of drugs, and these patients have lower long-term survival. Researchers tested whether adding two extra cancer drugs after surgery could help these poor responders live longer. They compared standard treatment in 310 patients with a stronger drug mix in 308 patients, and watched them for about five years. About half of patients in each group were alive without the cancer coming back at three years. The stronger drug mix did not improve the time patients stayed free of cancer events. It did cause more serious side effects, including more infections, kidney problems, and more second cancers. Because of this, the added drugs are not advised as routine care for these patients. Future progress will likely need new kinds of drugs and better ways to match treatment to each tumor.

Title: Nivolumab plus Ipilimumab versus Sunitinib in Advanced Renal-Cell Carcinoma
Abstract Summary: People with advanced kidney cancer often need strong drugs to help them live longer and feel better. Researchers compared two drug plans for adults with a common type of advanced kidney cancer. One plan used two immune drugs given through a vein, and the other used a daily pill drug. Over 1000 people took part, and they were placed into one of the two groups by chance. Many had cancer that was harder to treat and were watched for a little over two years. After 18 months, about 75 out of 100 people on the two immune drugs were still alive. About 60 out of 100 people on the pill drug were still alive at that time. Cancer shrank or went away in 42 out of 100 people on the two immune drugs. This happened in 27 out of 100 people on the pill drug. Side effects were common with both plans, but very bad ones were less often with the two immune drugs. These results suggest the two immune drugs may help some people with advanced kidney cancer live longer.
Full-Text Summary: People with advanced kidney cancer often get a drug called sunitinib as first treatment. Researchers compared sunitinib with a two‑drug immune treatment called nivolumab plus ipilimumab in adults with this cancer. Over 1000 people took part, and they were put into one of the two treatment groups by chance. Most had cancer with “intermediate” or “poor” outlook, which is linked to worse survival. In these higher‑risk patients, about 75 out of 100 were alive at 18 months with the immune pair. About 60 out of 100 were alive at 18 months with sunitinib alone, which is clearly lower. Tumors shrank in 42 out of 100 people on the immune pair, compared with 27 out of 100 on sunitinib. Tumors fully disappeared in 9 out of 100 on the immune pair, and 1 out of 100 on sunitinib. Serious treatment side effects were common with both options but were less frequent with the immune pair. People on the immune pair also reported better day‑to‑day well‑being scores than those on sunitinib. These results suggest the immune pair can help many higher‑risk kidney cancer patients live longer with better quality of life.

Title: Molecular Evolution of Early-Onset Prostate Cancer Identifies Molecular Risk Markers and Clinical Trajectories
Abstract Summary: Prostate cancer starts when cells in the prostate grow in an uncontrolled way and gain early DNA changesFinding these first changes can help sort men into higher or lower risk groups for future cancer growthResearchers studied prostate tumors from men age 55 or younger using several detailed lab tests on their DNAThey looked at 292 prostate cancer samples and tracked how DNA changes were linked with ageThey found a steady, clock like pattern of DNA damage that seemed to drive some of the first cancer changesThe team found four main types of prostate cancer based on these DNA patternsOne type was very aggressive and often had extra copies of a certain gene that was more active than normalThis aggressive type was confirmed in about 12,000 prostate tumor samples on glass slidesBy linking DNA patterns with risk groups, researchers mapped how prostate cancer may grow and change over timeThese results may help doctors better judge which men need stronger treatment and which can avoid extra care
Full-Text Summary: Prostate cancer can grow slowly in some men and very fast in others, especially when it starts at a young age. Researchers closely examined the DNA and other signals in 292 prostate tumors, including many from men age 55 or younger. They looked for early changes in tumor cells and grouped cancers into four main types based on these changes. One group had extra copies of a gene called ESRP1, which led to higher ESRP1 levels in the cancer cells. These tumors were linked to higher Gleason scores, more spread to lymph nodes, and faster cancer growth. High ESRP1 levels also matched with a higher chance of the cancer coming back after treatment. The team built a score, called PEPCI, using DNA marks to reflect how aggressive a tumor is. High PEPCI scores were tied to higher Gleason scores and a greater risk of cancer return. Using these data, they created a computer model to predict which DNA change is likely to happen next. This model also estimates how long a patient may stay free from signs of cancer return. In the future, these tools may help doctors better sort patients by risk and guide treatment choices.

Title: A deep learning system accurately classifies primary and metastatic cancers using passenger mutation patterns
Abstract Summary: Many people learn they have cancer only after it has already spread to other body parts. In about 3 out of 100 cases, doctors cannot find where the cancer first started. Researchers used a computer tool to study full DNA maps from 2,606 tumours from 24 common cancer types. They trained the tool to spot tiny DNA changes that do not directly drive cancer growth, called passenger changes. The tool guessed the cancer type correctly in 91 out of 100 tumours it had not seen before. On new main tumours, it was right 88 out of 100 times, and on spread tumours, 83 out of 100 times. This was about twice as accurate as trained cancer doctors when they saw only a spread tumour. Adding DNA changes that do drive cancer growth made the tool less accurate, which was unexpected. The pattern of small DNA changes seemed to hold key clues about where the cancer began. In the future, this kind of tool may help doctors find the source of hard to place cancers.
Full-Text Summary: Cancer doctors often need to know where a tumour first started in the body to choose the best treatment. Sometimes the cancer has already spread, and scans and lab tests cannot find the first tumour site. Researchers used DNA from 2,606 tumours from 24 common cancer types. They looked at many small DNA changes that do not drive the cancer but build up over time. A computer program learned patterns in these DNA changes to guess the cancer type. The program was right for 91 out of 100 tumours in the main group. In other groups from other labs, it was right for 88 out of 100 main tumours. For tumours that had spread, it was right for 83 out of 100 cases. The program worked better when it used many “passenger” DNA changes, not just key cancer genes. These results suggest DNA patterns can point to where a cancer began, even after it spreads. In the future, this kind of test might help guide care for people with cancers of unknown starting place.

Title: Pan-cancer analysis of whole genomes identifies driver rearrangements promoted by LINE-1 retrotransposition
Abstract Summary: Many cancer cells carry extra bits of jumping DNA that insert into their normal DNA. Researchers studied almost 3,000 tumor samples from 38 types of cancer to track these jumping DNA events. They found over 19,000 new jumping DNA events, and about one in three tumors had at least one event. In cancers of the food pipe, these events were the most common big DNA change seen in the cells. They were the second most common big DNA change in some head and neck and bowel cancers. Some jumping DNA events cut out very large parts of a chromosome, sometimes removing genes that usually slow cancer growth. They can also cause tangled swaps and extra copies of large DNA regions inside the cancer cell. In some cases, these changes lead to many extra copies of genes that push cells to grow and divide. Together, these findings show that jumping DNA can reshape cancer cell DNA in ways that help tumors form and grow. In the future, careful study of these DNA changes may help doctors better understand how some cancers start and change over time.
Full-Text Summary: Many cancer cells carry extra bits of DNA that can copy and paste themselves into new places in the genome. Researchers examined nearly 3,000 tumor and normal DNA samples from 38 cancer types to track these moving DNA pieces. They found over 19,000 new insertions, and about one in three tumors had at least one event. These events were especially common in cancers of the food pipe, head and neck, lung, and colon. Most insertions came from one type of jumping DNA, which can cut the genome and insert a new copy. In some tumors, these insertions were the most common kind of large DNA change. Many insertions landed inside genes, including 66 in known cancer‑related genes. Some insertions cut out huge stretches of DNA, up to tens of millions of letters long. These cuts sometimes removed “brake” genes that normally slow cancer, or increased copies of “gas pedal” genes that drive growth. Overall, a small number of very active jumping DNA sites caused most of this damage in certain cancers. Understanding these patterns may help explain how some tumors gain dangerous DNA changes and could guide future genome‑based tests.

Title: Patterns of somatic structural variation in human cancer genomes
Abstract Summary: Cancer cells often have big changes in their DNA, such as pieces deleted, copied, or moved around. Researchers studied DNA from 2,658 cancers from 38 types, using full genome reading tools. They grouped and labeled patterns of these DNA changes and found 16 main types, called signatures. Some changes remove pieces of DNA, and these deletions come in several common sizes and appear in certain cancer types. Other changes copy pieces of DNA in a row, and these copies also come in several common sizes. Some DNA changes happen when cells copy their DNA in a faulty way, which can create twisted and complex shapes. One common pattern uses 2 to 7 DNA pieces from different places, joined together in one spot. These joined pieces often appear with copied DNA runs and can turn on a key growth gene in liver cancer. Many different DNA change processes can shape how a cancer grows and which cells survive. In the future, these patterns may help doctors better sort cancers and choose more exact treatments.
Full-Text Summary: Cancer cells often have big changes in their DNA, where pieces are cut, copied, moved, or lost. Researchers examined whole DNA from 2,559 cancers from 38 types, using strict tests to find these large DNA changes. They grouped the changes into simple ones, like pieces deleted or copied in place, and complex ones with many linked breaks. Simple deletions were the most common, followed by copied segments placed next to the original and then pieces moved elsewhere. In many cancers, several copied DNA pieces were stitched together into one new stretch, sometimes using 2–7 different segments. These “copy and paste” events often added extra gene copies and could turn cancer‑promoting genes on or switch off protectors. For example, in liver cancer, 10 of 30 cases with changes in a key growth gene had these special copy‑and‑paste events. The team found 16 main patterns of these large DNA changes, each linked to different ways cells copy and repair DNA. Some patterns were tied to faults in known DNA repair genes, such as BRCA1, BRCA2, and related partners. These results help explain how many paths can lead to cancer and may guide future tests that match tumors to repair‑targeted drugs.

Title: Molecular Subsets in Renal Cancer Determine Outcome to Checkpoint and Angiogenesis Blockade
Abstract Summary: Kidney cancer can look very different from person to person, even when it has spread in the body. Researchers closely studied 823 kidney tumors to look for patterns in genes and other cell signals. They found seven main tumor types, each with its own way of growing blood vessels, using energy, and handling the immune system. Some tumors made many new blood vessels, while others showed strong immune attack or very fast cell growth. Two common drug plans were checked in these groups, one blocking blood vessel growth, and one mixing that with immune drugs. The mix with immune drugs helped more when tumors showed strong immune attack or very fast cell growth signals. Certain gene changes were linked to high blood vessel growth, while others were linked to fast cell growth and energy use. A hard to treat form, called sarcomatoid, had fewer blood vessel signs but more immune target signs on the tumor cells. This may explain why immune drugs often work better than blood vessel drugs alone in this form. These results may help doctors sort patients by tumor type and choose more personal treatment plans in the future.
Full-Text Summary: Kidney cancer called renal cell carcinoma is common and often deadly when it has spread in the body. Researchers studied 823 tumor samples from people with advanced kidney cancer in a large treatment trial. They looked at patterns of gene activity and gene changes in these tumors and grouped them into seven types. Some tumor types had strong blood vessel growth signals, while others showed fast cell growth or strong immune cell presence. People with tumors rich in blood vessel signals tended to do better on either of the two main drug options. People with tumors that grew faster and had more immune signals did better with the drug mix that included immune therapy. Certain gene changes were linked to better or worse outcomes and to which drug choice worked better. For example, changes in one gene were tied to longer time before the cancer grew again, no matter the drug. Other gene changes were linked to worse outlook, but these patients often did better with the immune drug mix. Tumors with a “sarcomatoid” pattern were very aggressive but often responded well to the immune drug mix. These results suggest that testing tumor gene patterns may help match future patients to the treatment most likely to help.

Title: Nivolumab plus Cabozantinib versus Sunitinib for Advanced Renal-Cell Carcinoma
Abstract Summary: People with advanced kidney cancer often need strong drugs to slow the disease and help them live longer. Researchers compared two treatment plans for adults who had not received past drug treatment for this cancer. One group took a mix of two drugs, given on a set schedule, and the other group took a single drug. There were 651 people in the trial, with about half in each group. The mix of two drugs kept the cancer from getting worse for about 16.6 months. The single drug kept the cancer from getting worse for about 8.3 months, which is about half as long. After one year, about 86 out of 100 people on the mix were still alive. About 76 out of 100 people on the single drug were still alive after one year. The cancer shrank or went away in about 56 out of 100 people on the mix. This happened in about 27 out of 100 people on the single drug. Serious side effects were common in both groups and sometimes led people to stop treatment. People on the mix of drugs reported better day to day well being than those on the single drug.
Full-Text Summary: People with advanced kidney cancer often need medicine to slow or stop tumor growth. Researchers compared two treatment plans for adults with this cancer who had not had drug treatment before. One plan used two drugs together, nivolumab and cabozantinib, and the other used one drug, sunitinib. A total of 651 people took part, with about half in each treatment group. Tumors stayed under control for a median of 16.6 months with the two-drug plan, and 8.3 months with sunitinib. After one year, about 86 out of 100 people on the two drugs were alive, versus about 76 out of 100 on sunitinib. Tumors shrank in about 56% of people on the two drugs, compared with about 27% on sunitinib. Serious side effects were common in both groups, in about three out of four people. About 20% of people on the two drugs stopped at least one drug because of side effects. People on the two-drug plan reported better day-to-day quality of life than those on sunitinib. These results suggest the two-drug plan may become an important first treatment choice for advanced kidney cancer.

Title: Integrated Machine Learning and Bioinformatic Analyses Constructed a Novel Stemness-Related Classifier to Predict Prognosis and Immunotherapy Responses for Hepatocellular Carcinoma Patients
Abstract Summary: Liver cancer called HCC is often hard to treat, even with new immune based drugs. A small group of cancer cells, called cancer stem cells, can help tumors start, spread, and resist many drugs. Researchers used large gene test sets from cancer and stem cell groups to study these special cells in HCC. They gave each liver tumor a “stemness score” that showed how much it acted like these strong starter cells. They then split patients into two groups based on this score, using a math method called clustering. These two groups had different immune cell patterns around the tumor and different gene activity linked to the immune system. They also showed different signs of how well early drug treatment before surgery might work. Four computer learning tools were used to tell these two groups apart more clearly. From this, researchers built a simple test based on five key genes to sort patients into the two groups. This new way to group liver cancer may help predict outcome and guide immune and targeted drug choices in the future.
Full-Text Summary: Liver cancer of the main type, called liver cell cancer, often has poor survival and few good drug choices. Some liver cancer cells act like stem cells, which means they can keep making new cancer cells and resist many drugs. Researchers used large gene activity datasets from hundreds of liver cancer patients to measure how “stem-like” each tumor was. They grouped patients into two stemness types and saw that one type had higher stemness scores and worse survival over time. This higher stemness type also showed signs of a weaker immune attack inside the tumor, called an immune cold state. The other type had stronger immune cell presence and higher levels of common immune “brake” proteins that immune drugs target. Patients in this lower stemness group were predicted to respond better to some immune drugs and a targeted pill called erlotinib. Researchers then built a simple lab test based on five genes to tell these two stemness types apart in new patients. This test worked well in two separate patient groups and could predict which patients lived longer. If confirmed in future trials, this stemness test might help doctors choose immune and targeted drugs more wisely for liver cancer.

Title: Neoadjuvant Nivolumab plus Chemotherapy in Resectable Lung Cancer
Abstract Summary: People with an early stage type of lung cancer often have surgery to remove the tumor, but cancer can return.
