Doctors sometimes give drug treatment before surgery to shrink the tumor and lower the chance it comes back. Researchers compared two plans for people with lung cancer that could be removed by surgery. One plan used a mix of a newer immune drug plus standard cancer drugs before surgery. The other plan used only standard cancer drugs before surgery. People who got the mix of drugs went about 31.6 months without the cancer growing or coming back. People who got only standard drugs went about 20.8 months without the cancer growing or coming back. In the mix group, about 24 out of 100 people had no live cancer cells left at surgery. In the standard group, about 2 out of 100 people had no live cancer cells left at surgery. Serious side effects were common but happened at about the same rate in both groups. Most people in both groups were still able to have surgery as planned. These results suggest adding the immune drug before surgery may better control this lung cancer without adding extra harm.
Full-Text Summary: People with early lung cancer often can have surgery, but the cancer still comes back in many cases. Doctors are testing if adding an immune drug to chemo before surgery can help people stay cancer free longer. Researchers gave one group chemo plus an immune drug called nivolumab, and another group chemo alone before surgery. They then compared how long people lived without the cancer growing or coming back, and how many had no cancer left at surgery. People who got nivolumab plus chemo went a median of 31.6 months without cancer events, versus 20.8 months with chemo alone. At one year, about 76% on the combo had no cancer return, compared with about 63% on chemo alone. At surgery, 24% of people on the combo had no live cancer cells, compared with about 2% on chemo alone. Serious treatment side effects were common in both groups, but were not higher with nivolumab plus chemo. Adding nivolumab also did not make surgery harder to do or more risky. These results suggest that chemo plus nivolumab before surgery may help some people with early lung cancer live longer without relapse. This approach is now an approved option for some adults with operable lung cancer in the United States.

Title: Trastuzumab Deruxtecan in Previously Treated HER2-Low Advanced Breast Cancer
Abstract Summary: Many people with breast cancer have tumors with only a small amount of a marker called HER2 on their cells. Current drugs that target HER2 do not work well for these “HER2-low” cancers, especially after other chemo has failed. Researchers tested a drug called trastuzumab deruxtecan in people with HER2-low breast cancer that had spread in the body. They compared this drug to the doctor’s choice of standard chemo in a large group of patients. Most people in the trial, about 89 out of 100, had tumors that also used hormone signals to grow. People who got trastuzumab deruxtecan went longer before their cancer grew again, about 10 months versus about 5 months. They also lived longer overall, about 24 months versus about 18 months with standard chemo. Looking at all patients together, the time without cancer growth and overall survival were also longer with this drug. Serious side effects were common with both treatments, but somewhat fewer people had them with trastuzumab deruxtecan. Some people on trastuzumab deruxtecan had serious lung problems, and a small number of these were fatal. These results suggest this drug may become an option for people with HER2-low metastatic breast cancer after earlier chemo.
Full-Text Summary: Many people with advanced breast cancer have low levels of a marker called HER2 on their tumor cells. These cancers are usually treated like HER2‑negative cancers and often have few good treatment options after first drugs stop working. Researchers tested a drug called trastuzumab deruxtecan in people with HER2‑low breast cancer that had spread in the body. They compared this drug with the doctor’s choice of standard chemo drugs in more than 550 people. People who got trastuzumab deruxtecan went about 10 months before the cancer grew, versus about 5 months with standard chemo. Overall survival was about 23 to 24 months with trastuzumab deruxtecan, compared with about 17 months with standard chemo. About half of patients had their tumors shrink with trastuzumab deruxtecan, compared with about 16% on standard chemo. Serious side effects happened in both groups, but were somewhat less common with trastuzumab deruxtecan than with standard chemo. A lung problem called lung inflammation or scarring occurred in about 12% of people on trastuzumab deruxtecan and was sometimes fatal. These results suggest trastuzumab deruxtecan could become an important treatment choice for many people with HER2‑low advanced breast cancer.

Title: Identification of Anoikis-Related Subgroups and Prognosis Model in Liver Hepatocellular Carcinom
Abstract Summary: Liver cancer can spread when cancer cells avoid a type of cell death called anoikis, which normally stops loose cells. The way this cell death works in liver cancer was not clear before this work. Researchers used large public cancer data sets to sort liver tumors into groups based on anoikis related genes. They then built a risk score using several key genes linked with this cell death process and patient survival time. This risk score was checked in other liver cancer data sets from around the world to see if it held up. The liver cancer cases fell into two main groups, and one group had clearly worse survival than the other. Five genes tied to anoikis were linked with how long people with liver cancer lived. The risk score based on these genes did a good job at predicting overall survival. The risk score also linked closely with certain immune cells found inside the tumors. These results may help explain how liver cancer grows and could guide new ways to plan treatment in the future.
Full-Text Summary: Liver cancer is a common and deadly cancer, and doctors still need better ways to predict how patients will do. Researchers studied a type of cell death called anoikis, which normally kills cells that lose their support in the body. Cancer cells can resist this death, stay alive, and spread to new places in the body. Using large public data sets, researchers looked at many liver tumors and nearby normal tissue. They found 168 genes linked to anoikis that were different in liver cancer tissue than in normal liver tissue. Based on these genes, they split patients into groups with different chances of survival. They then built a “risk score” using five key genes tied to anoikis and patient survival. People with a high risk score died sooner and more often than people with a low score. The score predicted one‑, three‑, and five‑year survival with good accuracy in several data sets. The five genes and the risk score were also linked to many types of immune cells in the tumor. These results suggest that anoikis‑related genes may help doctors judge outlook and guide care in liver cancer in the future.

Title: T-cell exhaustion signatures characterize the immune landscape and predict HCC prognosis via integrating single-cell RNA-seq and bulk RNA-sequencing
Abstract Summary: Liver cancer called hepatocellular carcinoma is a common cause of cancer death and often has a poor outlook. Researchers studied a type of immune cell problem called T cell loss, which happens when these cells are overworked for too long. This T cell loss is linked to how well the body can fight tumors and how long patients may live. Researchers used large sets of tumor gene data from many liver cancer patients to look for patterns of T cell loss. They built a gene “signature,” a group of 11 genes, that was strongly tied to patient survival in liver cancer. People placed in the low‑risk group by this gene test lived longer than those in the high‑risk group. The risk score stayed useful even when other clinical factors were taken into account. Tools that combined the risk score with basic clinical facts gave strong power to predict patient outcomes. This gene signature may help doctors judge which patients could respond better to immune‑based cancer drugs. In the future, this kind of test might guide more personal treatment plans for people with liver cancer.
Full-Text Summary: Liver cancer called hepatocellular carcinoma is common and often deadly, especially when found at a late stage. T cells are blood cells that should attack cancer, but in many patients they become tired and stop working well. Researchers used large gene data sets from hundreds of liver cancer patients to study this T cell tiredness process. They picked 11 key genes linked to tired T cells and built a “risk score” based on gene activity levels. Patients with a low risk score lived longer than those with a high risk score in both main data groups. The risk score stayed important even when age, tumor stage, and other clinic details were also tested. Patients with low scores often had lower gene mutation load and better survival than those with high scores. The score also related to which immune cells were inside the tumor and to many immune “brake” signals. In several groups of people given immune therapy, lower risk scores linked with better treatment response and survival. Some common chemo drugs also seemed to work differently in high and low risk groups. This gene-based risk score may help doctors sort liver cancer patients by outlook and guide immune or drug treatment choices.

Title: Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy combined with sequential perioperative toripalimab in locally advanced esophageal squamous cell cancer
Abstract Summary: People with a type of throat cancer called esophageal squamous cell cancer often need better treatment options. Researchers tested a plan that used both chemo, radiation, and an immune drug called toripalimab before and after surgery. They gave this plan to 21 adults with cancer in the chest part of the esophagus that could be removed. Most patients had the planned surgery after these treatments, while one person chose not to have surgery. Among 19 people with this cancer who had surgery, about 79% had very few cancer cells left in the tumor. In about 47% of these patients, no cancer cells were seen in the removed tumor at all. All 21 patients had some side effects, most often low white blood cell counts in the blood. About two thirds had more serious side effects, mainly very low levels of certain infection fighting cells. Three patients had the cancer come back, and people with a stronger tumor response stayed cancer free longer. Overall, this mix of chemo, radiation, surgery, and immune drug seemed helpful and acceptably safe for this cancer type. More time and follow up are needed to know how well people live in the long term.
Full-Text Summary: Cancer of the esophagus is common and often found at a late stage, when cure is hard. Researchers treated 21 adults with a mix of radiation, two cancer drugs, and an immune drug called toripalimab before and after surgery. Twenty people had surgery, and 19 with this cancer type were checked for how much tumor was left. About 79% of these 19 people had very little cancer left in the main tumor after treatment. About 47% had no signs of cancer in the removed tumor or nearby lymph glands. Most people had side effects like low white blood cells, but there were no treatment‑related deaths. Some people had surgery problems like leaks or lung infection, but these were similar to past reports. People whose tumors shrank more tended to stay free of cancer longer during the follow‑up time. Scans done after treatment helped tell who still had cancer and who likely had none left. This combined treatment looks helpful and fairly safe for people with this type of esophagus cancer that can be removed. Larger and longer studies are still needed to know the true long‑term benefits and best use in patients.

Title: Association of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists with risk of cancers-evidence from a drug target Mendelian randomization and clinical trials
Abstract Summary: Many people now use a newer type of drug to help with weight loss and type 2 diabetes. Researchers used people’s genetic data as a stand in for long term use of these drugs. They looked at links between this stand in and 14 common cancers in very large data sets. They also checked past clinical trials of these drugs to see how often cancer was reported. The genetic work showed a lower chance of breast cancer and a common skin cancer called basal cell cancer. It also showed a higher chance of colon and rectal cancer in people with this genetic pattern. There was no clear link with cancer of the ovary, lung, or thyroid gland. Across 80 clinical trials, very few people on these drugs were found to have any kind of cancer. Overall, the drugs may lower some cancer risks but may raise colon and rectal cancer risk. So far, cancer cases in people taking these drugs stay low, but careful watching is still needed. Future large and long term trials are needed to better judge cancer risk and benefit for patients.
Full-Text Summary: Many people now use a newer type of weight loss and diabetes drug that acts on a gut hormone receptor. Researchers used people’s genetic data to model long term effects of this drug target on 14 common cancers. They also reviewed 80 clinical trials where adults took these drugs and checked how many later got cancer. The genetic work linked this drug target with lower risk of breast cancer and a common skin cancer called basal cell cancer. It also linked the drug target with higher risk of colon and rectal cancer, which together are called colorectal cancer. The same work suggested no clear change in risk for lung, thyroid, or ovarian cancer. Across 65,328 people who took these drugs in trials, 1,559 later developed some type of cancer. In these trials, the most often seen cancers were pancreatic, breast, lung, colorectal, and prostate cancers, but numbers were small. Overall, cancer cases in people taking these drugs were low, but follow up time was often short. These results suggest possible trade offs in cancer risk and show the need for larger, long term trials.

Title: Lorlatinib Versus Crizotinib in Patients With Advanced ALK-Positive Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: 5-Year Outcomes From the Phase III CROWN Study
Abstract Summary: People with a certain type of lung cancer often see their disease grow again after first treatment. Researchers compared two daily pills for people with this lung cancer type who had not had past treatment. One pill was lorlatinib, taken once a day, and the other was crizotinib, taken twice a day. After about five years, cancer stayed under control much longer with lorlatinib than with crizotinib. The middle value for time without cancer growth was not yet reached for lorlatinib, but was 9.1 months for crizotinib. About 60 out of 100 people on lorlatinib had no cancer growth at five years, versus 8 out of 100 on crizotinib. Cancer spread in the brain also took much longer to appear with lorlatinib than with crizotinib. Side effects with lorlatinib were in line with what was seen in earlier checks. Blood tests at the end of lorlatinib treatment did not show new cancer gene changes linked to this drug. These results suggest lorlatinib may give people with this lung cancer longer control of their disease than older targeted pills.
Full-Text Summary: People with a certain type of advanced lung cancer often see their disease grow again after treatment. Researchers compared two daily pills, lorlatinib and crizotinib, in 296 people who had not had prior treatment. They watched how long people lived without their cancer getting worse, and how well the drugs protected the brain. After about five years, cancer stayed under control much longer with lorlatinib than with crizotinib. The middle value for time without cancer growth was over five years with lorlatinib, but only about nine months with crizotinib. About 60% of people on lorlatinib had no cancer growth at five years, compared with 8% on crizotinib. Lorlatinib also did a better job keeping cancer from starting or growing in the brain. Side effects were common with both drugs, and serious side effects were more frequent with lorlatinib. Most brain-related side effects with lorlatinib were mild to moderate and could be managed by changing the dose. These results suggest lorlatinib may offer longer control of this lung cancer, especially in protecting the brain.

Title: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy with or without camrelizumab in resectable esophageal squamous cell carcinoma: the randomized phase 3 ESCORT-NEO/NCCES01 trial
Abstract Summary: People with a certain type of throat and food pipe cancer often need strong treatment before surgery. Researchers tested if adding a new immune drug to standard chemo before surgery could help more patients. They worked with 391 adults who could still have surgery for this cancer in the chest area. People were split into three groups and all got two rounds of treatment, then surgery. Two groups got chemo plus the immune drug, and one group got chemo alone. The two immune drug groups also kept getting the immune drug after surgery for a time. The main goal was to see how many people had no cancer left in the removed tissue. About 28 out of 100 people in one immune drug group had no cancer seen after surgery. About 15 out of 100 people in the other immune drug group had no cancer seen. Only about 5 out of 100 people in the chemo alone group had no cancer seen. Serious side effects during treatment and after surgery were common but close in all three groups. Adding the immune drug to chemo before surgery cleared all seen cancer in more people, with side effects that doctors could manage.
Full-Text Summary: People with a type of throat tube cancer called esophageal squamous cell cancer often need treatment before surgery. Researchers tested if adding an immune drug called camrelizumab to standard chemo before surgery could kill more cancer cells. They split 391 adults into three groups and gave all of them two cycles of chemo before surgery. Two groups also got the immune drug before surgery and again after surgery, while one group got chemo only. In the chemo-only group, about 5 out of 100 people had no cancer left in the removed tissue. With chemo plus the immune drug, about 15 out of 100 and 28 out of 100 people had no cancer left. More people in the immune drug plus chemo groups also had very small amounts of cancer left after surgery. Side effects like low white blood cells were common in all groups and were somewhat higher with the added immune drug. Serious surgery problems and deaths within 30 or 90 days were low and similar across all groups. These results suggest that adding this immune drug to chemo before surgery may clear more cancer without making surgery less safe. Long-term survival results are not ready yet, so the effect on life span is still unknown.

Title: Phase 3 Trial of Stereotactic Body Radiotherapy in Localized Prostate Cancer
Abstract Summary: Men with early prostate cancer often get many weeks of daily radiation treatment. Researchers compared a short, focused radiation plan with the usual longer radiation plans in these men. They randomly placed 874 men into two groups at many cancer centers. One group got five radiation treatments over one to two weeks, and the other got 20 to 39 treatments over four to seven weeks. No one in either group was allowed to get hormone blocking drugs during this time. After about six years, about 96 out of 100 men in the short plan group had no cancer signs in blood or scans. About 95 out of 100 men in the longer plan group also had no cancer signs. The short plan caused more later urine side effects, about 27 out of 100 men, versus 18 out of 100 with longer plans. Bowel side effects were about the same in both groups, around 10 out of 100 men. Overall, the short plan worked as well as the longer plans for these early prostate cancers. These results suggest some men may finish radiation faster, with similar cancer control but somewhat higher urine side effects.
Full-Text Summary: Men with early prostate cancer often get many weeks of daily radiation treatment to cure the disease. Researchers compared a short course of focused radiation, given in five treatments, with the usual longer radiation plans. They enrolled 874 men with low or medium risk prostate cancer and randomly placed them into two treatment groups. One group had radiation over four to eight weeks, and the other group finished in one to two weeks. After about six years, about 95 out of 100 men in both groups had no signs of cancer coming back. The short course worked just as well as the longer course at keeping the cancer under control. More men in the short course group had lasting urine side effects, about 27% versus 18% with the longer course. Bowel and sexual side effects were low and very similar between the two groups over five years. Most men in both groups reported stable bladder and bowel control from two to five years after treatment. These results suggest that a five-treatment plan can be an effective option for many men with early prostate cancer. In the future, this shorter plan may offer good cancer control with fewer hospital visits for some patients.

Title: The Germline and Somatic Origins of Prostate Cancer Heterogeneity
Abstract Summary: Prostate cancer starts when cells in the prostate grow out of control and form a tumor. Researchers studied a very large group of prostate tumors to look for key gene changes that drive this cancer. They found 223 spots in the genes that were often changed in these tumors. These gene changes are called driver regions because they help the cancer grow and spread. Researchers also looked at gene changes people are born with and gene changes that happen later in life. They found links between these two kinds of gene changes and how fast the tumor became more serious. Some inherited gene changes seemed to shape which later gene changes appeared in the tumor. The timing of these later gene changes also seemed to affect how aggressive the cancer became. These findings help explain why prostate cancer can act very differently from one man to another. In the future, this kind of gene information may help doctors better predict which tumors will grow faster.
Full-Text Summary: Prostate cancer can be slow-growing in many men, but in some it becomes fast and life-threatening. Researchers examined 666 prostate tumors to map many kinds of DNA changes in each tumor. They looked at large and small DNA changes, and grouped tumors into seven genetic subtypes. Most tumors had about eight important DNA changes that helped the cancer grow and spread. High-grade tumors, which are more dangerous, had more total DNA changes than low-grade tumors. Certain early DNA changes, such as extra copies of growth genes, were more common in high-grade tumors. These early changes were linked with a higher chance of the cancer coming back after treatment. The pattern of DNA changes also related to common clinic tests, like blood PSA level and tumor size. Researchers then linked some inherited DNA markers with specific tumor DNA changes. They confirmed 11 such links in nearly 2,000 men, across early, localized, and advanced prostate cancer. Some of these inherited markers also changed how tumor DNA was switched on or off by chemical tags. In the future, these findings may help refine risk scores and guide how closely some men are watched.

Title: Darolutamide plus androgen-deprivation therapy: propensity score matching of ARASEC and historic clinical trial patients
Abstract Summary: Men with prostate cancer that has spread often get hormone blocking drugs, sometimes with a strong chemo drug called docetaxel. Some men cannot or do not want to get chemo, so another plan is needed. Researchers tested adding a pill called darolutamide to hormone blocking drugs, without chemo. They used past data from men who got only hormone blocking drugs as a comparison group. They made sure the two groups were as alike as possible at the start. They matched men by age, health, cancer spread, past treatment, and blood test levels. There were 223 men in the new treatment group and 393 men in the past group. Careful matching led to 160 men in each group with very similar health features. The groups will be used to check how well the new pill plus hormone blocking drugs work and how safe it is. This type of study may help test new cancer drugs faster and at lower cost in the future.
Full-Text Summary: Men with advanced prostate cancer often get a hormone-blocking treatment called ADT as their first main therapy. Researchers are testing if adding a pill called darolutamide to ADT can help these men live longer without cancer growth. They gave darolutamide plus ADT to 223 men in the United States with cancer that had spread but still responded to hormones. They then compared these men to 160 similar men from an older trial who had received ADT alone. The two groups were carefully matched by age, cancer spread, prior treatment, cancer grade, and blood marker levels. Earlier large trials showed that darolutamide with ADT, with or without chemotherapy, cut the risk of death by over 30%. Another trial without chemotherapy showed a 46% lower risk of cancer growth or death with darolutamide plus ADT. Side effects were similar between people who took darolutamide and those who took placebo, including tiredness and treatment stops. This new trial design uses past patient data to speed up testing and lower costs while still giving fair comparisons. Results from this work may support darolutamide plus ADT as another treatment choice for men with this type of prostate cancer.

Title: APOBEC3 mutagenesis drives therapy resistance in breast cancer
Abstract Summary: Many people with breast cancer get drug treatment, but over time the cancer can stop responding and grow again. Researchers studied 3,880 breast cancer samples to look for patterns in gene changes linked to this drug resistance. They focused on a group of body enzymes, called APOBEC3, that can cause many small changes in cancer cell genes. These APOBEC3 gene change patterns were common in breast cancers that had already been treated with hormone drugs. People with these patterns in hormone type breast cancer had shorter time before the cancer grew again on combined drugs. Lab tests and gene maps from main and spread tumors showed APOBEC3 activity helped cancers resist treatment. In some cases, APOBEC3 changes removed a key “brake” gene that normally helps control cell growth. Signs of APOBEC3 activity were also seen before treatment, showing it can shape breast cancer from early on. Overall, APOBEC3 activity often helps breast cancer escape treatment and keep growing. In the future, tests that detect APOBEC3 patterns might help predict which cancers will resist certain drugs.
Full-Text Summary: Many breast cancers stop responding to hormone and targeted drugs over time because their DNA keeps changing and adapting. Researchers studied DNA from 3,880 breast tumors and found a common pattern of damage linked to a group of enzymes called APOBEC3. These enzymes normally help fight viruses but can also cause many small DNA changes in cancer cells. The APOBEC3 pattern was seen often in advanced breast cancers, especially those that had already been treated. Tumors with this pattern tended to have more DNA damage and more total mutations than other tumors. In lab tests, turning on APOBEC3 enzymes in breast cancer cells caused many new DNA changes and made drug resistance appear faster. These DNA changes often hit genes that control growth signals or response to hormone drugs, helping the cancer survive treatment. Patients whose tumors showed strong APOBEC3 activity had shorter time before the cancer grew again on standard hormone plus targeted drugs. APOBEC3 activity was often present early, before treatment, and then increased over time as the cancer evolved. In the future, tests that read this DNA damage pattern might help flag breast cancers more likely to resist treatment and guide drug choices.

Title: Randomized Phase II Study of Concurrent Versus Sequential Pembrolizumab in Combination With Chemoradiation in Locally Advanced Head and Neck Cancer
Abstract Summary: People with some head and neck cancers often get both radiation and strong cancer drugs at the same time. Researchers tested adding an immune drug called pembrolizumab either during this treatment or after it was done. They worked with 80 adults who had advanced head and neck cancer, many with disease that had spread to neck nodes. Half got the immune drug starting one week before radiation and chemo, and half started two weeks after finishing them. After one year, cancer control without growth was higher when the immune drug was given after the main treatment, 84% versus 71%. After four years, cancer in the head and neck area stayed controlled in 96% of people in the later group, versus 64% in the early group. More immune cells that can weaken the body’s defense were seen in tumors when the drug was given during radiation and chemo. Giving the immune drug after chemo and radiation met the goals set for safety and cancer control and was chosen for more testing. These results suggest that timing of immune drugs with standard treatment may affect long term control of this cancer.
Full-Text Summary: People with some head and neck cancers often get both radiation and strong cancer drugs at the same time, called chemoradiation. Doctors also now use a type of immune treatment drug called pembrolizumab for some head and neck cancers. Researchers wanted to learn if pembrolizumab works better when given during chemoradiation or after it is finished. Eighty people with advanced head and neck cancer were put into two groups by chance. One group got pembrolizumab starting one week before chemoradiation and continuing during and after treatment. The other group finished chemoradiation first, then started pembrolizumab two weeks later. Both groups met safety and benefit goals set before the trial started. After four years, cancer control in the head and neck area was 96% with later pembrolizumab and 64% with earlier use. Survival without cancer growth and overall survival were also higher with later pembrolizumab, though not clearly proven. Serious side effects were common in both groups, but dose‑limiting problems were seen only with earlier pembrolizumab. These results suggest starting pembrolizumab after chemoradiation may give better long‑term control for these patients. Larger trials are needed to know if this approach should change standard care in the future.

Title: Leveraging sequences missing from the human genome to diagnose cancer
Abstract Summary: Cancer cells can release tiny bits of DNA into the blood, which can help with finding cancer early. Current blood tests that look at this DNA have some limits and can miss cancer or give unclear results. Researchers built a new way to read this blood DNA by looking for rare short DNA patterns called neomers. These neomers are made by cancer cells and are usually not found in people without cancer. The new method could tell who had cancer, even in early stages, and tell different cancer types apart. When tested on over 2,500 tumor samples from 21 cancer types, it beat other leading methods at sorting tumor types. In 465 blood samples, it found lung and ovarian cancer with high accuracy, with scores near 0.9 out of 1.0. The method also helped spot gene changes that may turn other genes on or off in cancer cells. Overall, this work points to a blood test that is simple, sharp, and can find cancer-linked DNA changes. In the future, this kind of test might help doctors find some cancers earlier and choose better care.
Full-Text Summary: Cancer cells release tiny bits of DNA into the blood, called cell-free DNA, that can be read by lab tests. Researchers looked for short DNA codes that almost never appear in healthy people but are created by cancer changes. They studied DNA from 2,577 tumors of 21 cancer types and found many of these special codes, called neomers. Each cancer type had its own pattern of neomers, which allowed computer models to tell cancer types apart with about 99% accuracy. Researchers then tested blood from 200 people with lung cancer and 180 people without cancer. Using neomers in blood DNA, they detected lung cancer with an accuracy score, called AUC, of 0.93 overall and 0.94 in early stage one. In 70 people with ovarian cancer and 123 controls, the test reached AUC 0.89 overall and 0.93 in early stages. Lab tests also showed that some neomers change how nearby genes are turned on or off, which may affect tumor behavior. With more testing and standard rules for sample handling, neomer blood tests might one day help find some cancers earlier and guide care.

Title: Senescent fibroblasts secrete CTHRC1 to promote cancer stemness in hepatocellular carcinoma
Abstract Summary: Liver cancer can grow and spread with help from nearby support cells that have stopped dividing but do not die. These support cells sit around the tumor and can change how the cancer behaves in the body. Researchers used large gene data sets from many people with liver cancer to study these support cells. They built a risk score based on ten genes linked to these aging support cells in liver tumors. People with a higher score had worse survival and more signs that their cancer cells could regrow and spread. The score also matched changes in the immune system, with more cells that weaken immune attack on the tumor. People with a low score had fewer gene changes in their tumors and responded better to some liver cancer treatments. One gene in the score, called CTHRC1, was much higher in these aging support cells. Lab and animal tests showed that this gene helped liver cancer cells stay “stem like” and move to new sites. The gene was turned on through a chain of signals inside the cell that can be blocked in theory. In the future, this risk score and the CTHRC1 gene might help guide liver cancer care and new drug targets.
Full-Text Summary: Liver cancer often returns and spreads because some cancer cells act like “seed” cells that can regrow the tumor. Inside liver tumors, there are support cells called fibroblasts that can grow old and stop dividing, a state called senescence. Researchers studied these old fibroblasts in liver tumors and called them senescent fibroblasts, or SCAFs. They used large gene data sets and lab tests in cells and mice to see how SCAFs affect cancer. SCAFs were the most “aged” cells in the tumor area and were strongly linked to these seed-like cancer cells. When liver cancer cells were grown with fluid from SCAFs, the cancer cells grew faster, spread more, and resisted drugs. In mice, tumors mixed with SCAFs were larger and spread to the lungs more often than tumors with normal fibroblasts. The team built a ten-gene score, called CSscore, that separated patients into high- and low-risk groups for survival. Patients with lower scores tended to live longer and responded better to some liver cancer treatments and immune drugs. A protein called CTHRC1, made in high amounts by SCAFs, helped drive cancer growth and spread through a signal chain called Notch1. Blocking CTHRC1 in SCAFs reduced tumor size and lung spread in mice, and lowered stem-like cancer traits. If confirmed in more people, this score and CTHRC1 might help guide treatment choices for liver cancer patients.

Title: Phase 2 Study of Monotherapy with Pembrolizumab for Advanced Adrenocortical Carcinoma
Abstract Summary: People with adrenocortical cancer often do not get good results from standard chemo drugs. Researchers tested a type of immune treatment called pembrolizumab in adults with advanced adrenocortical cancer. They gave the drug through a vein every three weeks, after stopping other cancer drugs. Twenty three people joined, with a middle age of 54 years. Of the 20 people who could be checked, six were alive and without cancer growth at 27 weeks. Four people had their tumors shrink, and this benefit lasted about 18 months on average. Overall, the middle time before the cancer grew again was four months. The middle time people stayed alive was about 15 and a half months. Three people had serious side effects linked to the drug, but no one died from the treatment. The drug gave clear benefit, such as tumor shrinkage or stable disease, in about 30 percent of patients. These results suggest this immune drug may help some people with this rare cancer, with side effects that can be managed.
Full-Text Summary: Cancer of the adrenal gland, called ACC, is rare and often grows fast, and usual drugs do not work well. Researchers gave a drug called pembrolizumab through a vein every three weeks to adults with advanced ACC. All 23 people had tried at least one other cancer treatment before getting this drug. Among 20 people who could be checked, 6 were alive and their cancer had not grown at about 6 months. Four of these 20 people had their tumors shrink, and the average time this lasted was about 18 months. On average, people lived about 4 months before the cancer grew again and about 15 months overall. Only three people had serious side effects linked to the drug, and no one died from the treatment. These results suggest this drug may help some people with advanced ACC and has side effects that doctors can usually manage. Future work may test this drug with other cancer drugs to see if more patients can benefit.
